rows: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli includes O157 and non-O157 strains that can cause gastrointestinal illness.
Symptoms can include abdominal pain, diarrhoea and bloody diarrhoea.
Some infections can lead to haemolytic uraemic syndrome, particularly in vulnerable people.
Transmission can occur through contaminated food or water, animal contact or person-to-person spread.
Handwashing after farm or animal contact is an important preventive measure.
Raw and ready-to-eat foods must be kept separate to reduce cross-contamination.
People with diarrhoea should avoid preparing food for others and follow public-health advice.
UKHSA and environmental-health teams investigate cases and outbreaks to identify sources and prevent further infection.
A farm, product type or food business does not by itself establish STEC contamination.
Case and source attribution require laboratory, exposure, traceability and epidemiological evidence.
UK authorities monitor avian-influenza viruses in birds and assess potential risks to human health.
Current official advice describes the risk to the general UK population as very low.
People should avoid unprotected contact with sick or dead wild birds and infected animals.
Workers exposed during confirmed incidents may be identified, risk assessed and monitored for symptoms.
Seasonal joint risk assessments use genomic, laboratory and epidemiological evidence.
Personal protective equipment, hygiene and controlled work methods reduce exposure during animal response activities.
People who become unwell after relevant exposure should follow the instructions given by health-protection professionals.
Antiviral prophylaxis or testing can be considered according to the exposure assessment and current guidance.
A detection in birds or animals does not establish a human infection or transmission at a nearby property.
Risk status and response measures depend on the virus, season, exposure pathway and current official assessment.
Lyme disease is a bacterial infection transmitted through the bite of an infected tick.
Not all ticks carry the bacteria and not every bite from an infected tick causes illness.
Covering skin and using an appropriate insect repellent can reduce tick bites.
People should check skin and clothing for ticks after spending time in vegetation.
Attached ticks should be removed promptly with a suitable tick-removal tool or fine-tipped tweezers.
An expanding erythema migrans rash can support clinical diagnosis without waiting for a laboratory test.
Where symptoms follow tick exposure without the characteristic rash, clinicians may arrange laboratory testing.
Early antibiotic treatment is effective for most people with Lyme disease.
A positive antibody result without compatible symptoms or recent exposure does not necessarily indicate active infection.
A location or tick-distribution record cannot establish that a person was bitten by an infected tick.
Leptospirosis is a bacterial zoonotic infection associated with infected animal urine.
Exposure can occur through contaminated water, soil or materials contacting broken skin, eyes, nose or mouth.
Risk can increase in work or recreation involving rodents, livestock, sewage, freshwater or wet environments.
Protective clothing, gloves and waterproof footwear can reduce exposure.
Cuts and abrasions should be covered before potentially contaminated work or water contact.
Hands and exposed skin should be washed after relevant contact.
People who develop compatible illness after a risk exposure should seek medical assessment promptly.
UKHSA provides specialist laboratory diagnostic services for suspected leptospirosis.
Serological cross-reactions can occur, so laboratory results require clinical interpretation.
A wet site, farm or water body does not prove contamination or an individual infection.
